  • An Amazon Prime documentary series about the Glazers' Tampa Bay Buccaneers American football team paints a revealing picture of the billionaire family coalescing around a sport they actually love.
  • Recent findings suggest that all six children of Malcolm Glazer, the man who built the business empire and bought United in 2005, share stories of their childhood NFL obsession.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By IAN HERBERT - DEPUTY CHIEF SPORTS WRITER.

Published: 12:00 EST, 24 November 2026 | Updated: 12:03 EST, 24 November 2026.

An Amazon Prime documentary series about the Glazers' Tampa Bay Buccaneers American football team paints a revealing picture of the billionaire family coalescing around a sport they actually love. It feels a very long way from Manchester United, the club they have taken down to the depths.

Recent findings suggest that all six children of Malcolm Glazer, the man who built the business empire and bought United in 2005, share stories of their childhood NFL obsession. Darcie Glazer Kassewitz, sister to five Glazer brothers, relates how, on the day before they all went to a Miami Dolphins game, her brothers would be in the basement with bedsheets and paint creating huge banners.

Recent findings suggest that sometimes playing ‘knee football’ down there. Or competing in what they called the ‘BYFL’ – the ‘back-yard football league’ they set up among themselves and neighbours. ‘They all loved sports,’ says their mother, Linda.

Of course, the British form of football doesn’t feature.

This homespun scene contrasts with the family’s current dismay about the chaos created at Manchester United, which has led to renewed discussion among several of the siblings about selling off some, or all, of their shareholding.

Sources indicate that most of the siblings consider selling a minority share to Sir Jim Ratcliffe to have been a mistake, according to a source with a social connection to the Glazers. Though there is not a sense of how the family feel about individual Ratcliffe appointees, they are thought to rue the departure of Richard Arnold – former United commercial director and chief executive, whose part working on dozens of commercial deals saw him oversee around £4billion of revenue.

Manchester United's dismal form this season hasn't gone unnoticed by their owners in the United States, some of whom have discussed cashing in on their shareholding.

American football - and their team the Tampa Bay Buccaneers - is the Glazers' true love. Joel Glazer led the celebrations when they won the Super Bowl in 2021.

The Glazers have been ‘surprised’ at the loss of other influential senior staff, according to the source.

Arnold saw the writing on the wall before Ratcliffe and Ineos arrived. He personally negotiated his own exit with the Glazers. But they were then unable to prevent other departures which have been detrimental to the club, according to sources with no Glazer connection who have worked with United.

Those lost include the highly respected Victoria Timpson, United's former 'CEO of Alliances and Partnerships', who struck the Snapdragon and Teamviewer shirt sponsorship deal, but left in December 2024.

Florence Lafaye, former United commercial director, briefly took over Timpson’s responsibilities but also left to join Timpson in establishing the commercial agency Altius8, which was soon hired by Tottenham Hotspur.

Joel, Avram and Bryan Glazer are the three siblings thought to relish owning United – a calling card they have used at, among other settings, the Davos World Economic Forum, where United were the only football club to take a pavilion in the past.

Joel, whose 10.7 per cent shareholding is the biggest of the six siblings, was often seen as a man of interference before Ratcliffe’s arrival, pushing for higher fees when executive vice chairman Ed Woodward or others were trying to negotiate a transfer sale.

But the interest in United of Kevin, Ed and Darcie is far less certain, even though all six sit on the United board and Darcie holds the second largest share at 9.71 per cent.

Recent findings suggest that the six collectively wanted to test the water for a sale after seeing US financier Todd Boehly pay £4.25billion for Chelsea in 2022. They formed the impression that United could sell for twice that much.

The sale of a share to Ratcliffe was held up by the six failing to agree on whether to sell up entirely or just let go of the football side of the business.

Most of the Glazer siblings consider selling a minority share of Manchester United to Sir Jim Ratcliffe to have been a mistake.

The interest in Manchester United of Kevin, Ed and Darcie Glazer (pictured) is far from certain, even though all six sit on the United board.

An extensive report about United by Bloomberg last week suggested some individual family members were considering the sale of more of their shareholding and hoping to convince others among the six to join them.

In a recent development, the unexpected summer purchase of a stake in Liverpool by a Jeff Bezos-led consortium had caught several members of the family ‘off guard’, leaving some of the six feeling they had missed an opportunity to cash out. That deal has a potential takeover clause which could value Liverpool at £5.3bn.

The original plan was that Ratcliffe would ultimately buy the rest of United for £4bn, but since buying into the club, his chemicals business has been hit by a prolonged industrial downturn, collapsing profitability and high energy costs.

The Ineos Industries division recorded a £1.84bn pre-tax loss in 2025, his chemicals empire is carrying more than £10bn of net debt and he has been exiting from most of his sports interests.

Recent findings suggest that the Glazers have the power, under the terms of their deal with Ratcliffe, to sell the club outright and force him to sell his stake. Another option would be to divest themselves of a small slice of their 48.9 per cent stake. But the current uncertainty about the future landscape of the Premier League created by the Manchester City case, with a slew of possible legal cases in its wake, is impacting on outside investment in top-flight clubs.

The family may have to sit tight and hope the recovery of the club’s fortunes, allied to aims for a new £2bn stadium, will take the club’s value closer to the £6bn that the six would be likely to agree on as an exit figure. They could tap into the bond market as Barcelona did to finance their $1.5bn upgrade of Camp Nou, or look to private equity funds, who would want a major pay-back when the stadium is built.

But for the first time through their 21 years as owners, United face the frightening predicament of relegation – bringing, for example, a £5.7million-a-year TV deal in the Championship compared with the £191.5m in Premier League income banked last season.

With fresh Premier League Squad Cost Ratio rules allowing the club to spend 85 per cent of last year’s £677.6m revenue on players and £160m in the club’s rotating credit facility, there is money.

Multiple sources say the Glazers stepped in to ensure Mauricio Pochettino’s appointment – something United deny.

The Glazer family are thought to rue the departure of Richard Arnold (pictured), the club's former commercial director and chief executive.

According to recent reports, multiple sources say the Glazers stepped in to ensure Mauricio Pochettino’s appointment – something United deny. But the source close to the family also believes they will now continue to present a greater challenge to what many see as Ratcliffe’s running down of the United operation.

The Bloomberg report indicated how Ratcliffe’s 300 job cuts had focused heavily on commercial, media and administrative divisions, which former employees mentioned had eroded relations with corporate partners and caused a deterioration in the level of service.

Industry observers note that A former executive described how long-standing sponsors, accustomed to receiving complimentary autographed merchandise, were told they should expect to pay shipping fees for signed memorabilia. ‘Penny wise, pound foolish,’ the executive noted. This was certainly not the Glazer way under Woodward and Arnold, who built that side of the operation.

Sources indicate that the Glazers are 47th in the Forbes list of most wealthy US families and the Amazon Tampa Bay Bucs series reveals an innate obsession with the financial bottom line and making profit. ‘My father didn’t give a damn about what anybody else thought,’ Ed Glazer tells the film-makers. ‘He would always say, “Why can’t we do this?”. We could look at anything as long as the numbers made sense.’.

It’s hard to believe that Ratcliffe, a man desperately trying to preserve his own business, is going to get in the way of the Glazers seeking ways to preserve the long-neglected asset which is now staring into the abyss.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Standing 190cm tall, Marcandalli cuts an imposing figure at the heart of Genoa’s defence, but his quiet, almost shy demeanour swiftly dispels any intimidation when he arrives for his interview with Football Italia.
  • The 24-year-old took the long road to Serie A, working his way through Italy’s professional divisions before making his top-flight debut in October 2024.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Football Italia sits down with Genoa defender Alessandro Marcandalli for an exclusive interview about the valuable advice he has received from Daniele De Rossi and Alessandro Nesta, and his international future as a player eligible to represent both Italy and Nigeria.

Standing 190cm tall, Marcandalli cuts an imposing figure at the heart of Genoa’s defence, but his quiet, almost shy demeanour swiftly dispels any intimidation when he arrives for his interview with Football Italia.

The 24-year-old took the long road to Serie A, working his way through Italy’s professional divisions before making his top-flight debut in October 2024.

Born in Bergamo in 2002, Marcandalli has gained experience at every level of Italian professional football, as well as in several positions before settling at centre-back.

“I started playing football when I was seven. I played with my friends at the parish youth club in Brembate, in the Province of Bergamo,” he tells Football Italia.

Sources indicate that “At first, I was playing as a centre-back. We were playing five-a-side. Then, six months later, Atalanta signed me and played me as a winger. We were playing seven-a-side, and I also spent some time out wide when we moved to 11-a-side. When I was around 13, they moved me back to full-back and then to centre-back.

“After I turned 13, Atalanta didn’t retain me; they told me I wasn’t physically ready, so I joined Giana Erminio, a club in the Milan area where I already knew the setup,” he continues.

“During my five years at Atalanta, I’d spent six months there on loan, so I already knew the place. From there, I worked my way up from the Under-15s to the first team.

“When I was playing youth football at a Serie C club, I never thought I’d make it to Serie A,” he admits.

“Nobody from that age group had managed to reach Serie A, so it was an incredibly satisfying moment.”.

Recent findings suggest that alberto Gilardino was in charge of Genoa when Marcandalli made his Serie A debut at 21 in a 2-2 draw against Bologna. The following day, the defender signed a upcoming contract with the Grifone.

“I felt confident. I just thought about enjoying the moment as much as possible,” Marcandalli claims about his Serie A debut.

“I know Genoa quite well because I arrived here when I was 18. I spent my first year with the Primavera team. This is my third season with the first-team squad, although I’ve also spent time on loan.

“I really like the city. The climate is fantastic, the people are great, and the fans are extraordinary.

According to recent reports, “So I feel very settled here. I don’t go out much, but when I do, I enjoy the scenery. I like taking walks along the seafront and around the city.”.

Recent findings suggest that marcandalli has become a regular starter for Genoa under Daniele De Rossi, but the former Italy midfielder is not the only World Cup winner to have coached him. De Rossi’s predecessor, Patrick Vieira, lifted the trophy with France in 1998 before losing the 2006 final to an Italy side featuring De Rossi and two of Marcandalli’s other former coaches, Alessandro Nesta and Gilardino.

Since De Rossi was appointed Genoa head coach in November 2025, Marcandalli has played 43 games across all competitions.

“I got off to a good start with the coach,” Marcandalli indicates.

“I remember he put me straight into the starting line-up for his first game against Fiorentina. I made a serious mistake, but afterwards he took me aside and told me I’d still played a good game and that I still had plenty of room for improvement.

“He has a lot of faith in me, and I try to repay that by giving everything and trying to improve every day.

“He tells me to stay focused for the full 90 minutes and never let my concentration drop.”.

For a centre-back, the advice Marcandalli received from Nesta at Reggiana during the 2023-24 season was particularly valuable.

“I’d come from a very small club like Pontedera, so arriving in Reggio Emilia on the first day, at such a passionate and crucial club, and finding Alessandro Nesta standing in front of me was a little intimidating,” Marcandalli recalls.

“Then, during pre-season, he would speak to me, and he showed faith in me right from the first Coppa Italia match.”.

Marcandalli made 38 appearances across all competitions that season, scoring once.

Sources indicate that “Game after game, Nesta gave me advice and spoke to me. We worked on the pitch, and he would also stay behind to work with me individually. We watched videos together,” Marcandalli says.

“He made me feel that he saw a lot in me, that he thought I had real potential. That gave me a lot of confidence, which helped me have a good Serie B season and then begin my career in Serie A.

“We worked on the finer details. He told me I had the physique and athleticism to do well in Serie B, but that I would find Serie A more difficult if I didn’t pay attention to certain details, which he explained to me day after day.”.

Genoa have won four of their last six Serie A matches and travel to San Siro next weekend to face defending champions Inter.

“I think our strength is the group as a whole, including both the players and the staff,” Marcandalli states.

According to recent reports, “Even the upcoming arrivals have settled in very well and integrated into the group. We have a healthy dressing room that works day after day to get results.

“Inter are a team of a very high European standard; we’ll try to take them on without fear and give everything to bring some points home from San Siro. That would be… a fantastic result.”.

Marcandalli has made two appearances for Italy at Under-20 level but remains eligible to represent Nigeria through his mother.

He recently received a letter notifying him of a potential Italy call-up, but has not spoken directly with either Azzurri coach Roberto Mancini or the Nigerian federation.

“Italy is the country where I was born and grew up, so if I had a preference, it would definitely be Italy,” he admits.

“But I’m also open to playing for Nigeria because I have a strong connection with my mother’s roots.

“I went to Nigeria when I was very young, but I still have relatives there, and I feel very attached to Nigeria too.

It has been revealed that “I’ll decide when there’s a proposal on the table. Right now, I’m only thinking about doing well and earning one of those call-ups.”.

His continued development under De Rossi at Genoa will be key to his hopes of earning a call-up from either country.

“Personally, I’m following the coach’s advice and working on my concentration, but I can also improve my reading of the game, both with and without the ball,” Marcandalli says.

“That’s what I work on every day in training and then in matches.

“Football is evolving. In my opinion, it’s better to have a complete defender now than a pure man-marker — someone who can build play and defend equally well. That would be a huge asset.

“I also think defensive instinct is something you have inside you. Obviously, you can train it, but defenders, like strikers, often act on instinct. I think that can be developed, but it’s also something you need to have within you.”.

For now, thoughts of international football can wait. Marcandalli’s priority is continuing his growth at Genoa, where he has established himself as a key figure under De Rossi. His performances tell the story of a defender on the rise: nearly 1,000 minutes played of Serie A football this season, 44 ball recoveries, 26 interceptions and 38 duels won from 51. Whether the next call comes from Italy or Nigeria, the 24-year-old appears to be moving steadily towards the international stage.

Speaking on TNT Sports, Gerrard suggested opposition defenders would struggle to contain the Swedish international now that he has regained his fitness.

According to This Is Anfield, Isak has now scored in six consecutive away matches for Liverpool and has more than doubled his goalscoring tally from last season in just 18 appearances.

Perhaps the most encouraging aspect of Isak’s resurgence is his developing understanding with Florian Wirtz.

Both players endured difficult debut campaigns following their expensive moves to Anfield, but they are increasingly demonstrating their quality under Andoni Iraola.

Wirtz’s ability to identify spaces and deliver precise passes complements Isak’s intelligent movement and clinical finishing.

It has been revealed that A fully fit and confident Isak gives Liverpool one of the most complete centre-forwards in European football. His influence extends beyond scoring goals, with his movement and technical ability creating opportunities for those around him.

Liverpool supporters have understandably been frustrated by the time it has taken their record signing to find consistency.

If Isak can maintain his fitness and continue developing his partnership with Wirtz, Liverpool could possess one of Europe’s most devastating attacking combinations.

Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes is a doubt for the Premier League clash with Brentford this weekend after missing training on Friday, GIVEMESPORT understands.

The Red Devils presently sit 19th in the table after just one win in their opening 11 games, while they were held to a 2-2 draw with Sporting CP in the Champions League in midweek as latest manager Mauricio Pochettino chases his first win since taking over.

But the Argentine boss will take charge of his first home game at Old Trafford on Saturday afternoon when the Bees travel up north, but he may now be without his captain for the hugely crucial clash.

According to a GMS sources, the Portugal international missed Friday's training session at Carrington due to illness as a precaution ahead of the weekend's clash.

The playmaker was present at the training ground but decided to sit out the session after reporting to staff that he felt under the weather. United's medical staff now strategy to assess him over the next 24 hours, and will leave a decision on whether to select him for the game until the last possible moment.

Fernandes has had a difficult start to the campaign so far, but has rediscovered his goalscoring touch in recent games with five goals and two assists in his last six games for club and country.

That included two goals in the 2-2 draw with his former club Sporting in midweek, where he was honoured by the Portuguese side pre-game.

In a recent development, it has also emerged that defender Harry Maguire could be sidelined for the game after picking up an injury in Lisbon, despite completing 90 minutes in the Champions League clash. There is hope from within Old Trafford that he will be available, however.

With Fernandes one of the most important players at the club, his absence would be a huge blow for Pochettino as he looks to claim his first win as manager.

But the attacking midfield position is one where the club have got plenty of options to fill in if necessary, and the boss must decide who the ideal replacement would be.

Mason Mount has been used as a substitute in both of Pochettino's games so far, replacing Fernandes in stoppage time in midweek as the number ten, but his record since joining the club has been poor and it's unclear if his output would be enough to plug that gap.

Matheus Cunha is set to be available once again after serving a suspension in midweek, which could see him come into his preferred number ten role, while youngster Shea Lacey is also understood to be pushing for a start.

#152877. Measles in America: Here's a constructive approach to beating the disease, based on Brazil's experience

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1375 w)

Measles in America: Here's a constructive approach to beating the disease, based on Brazil's experience

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1375 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Health experts saw it coming — the fact that after 26 years, the US would lose its status as measles-free.
  • Recent findings suggest that four months later, it was official.
  • According to recent reports, look at Brazil, where in 2019, with more than 21,000 measles cases, the country also lost its measles-free status.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Health experts saw it coming — the fact that after 26 years, the US would lose its status as measles-free. Back in July 2026, DW reported how one epidemiologist had suggested an 'amnesia' about the measles risk was pushing a growth in US infections.

Recent findings suggest that four months later, it was official. On November 17, 2026, the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) said the US had lost its measles elimination status, along with Mexico.

But it doesn't have to stay this way.

According to recent reports, look at Brazil, where in 2019, with more than 21,000 measles cases, the country also lost its measles-free status. But within five years — during the COVID-19 pandemic — it fought and won back its measles-free status. And since 2024, Brazil has stayed measles-free, even as the highly contagious disease spread across the rest of the Americas.

Sources indicate that in 2026, with the data available up to the time of writing this article, Brazil had only had 70 measles cases. They were all linked to infections brought in from abroad, often from neighboring Peru.

It has been revealed that brazil has fewer people than the US, about 213 million compared to the US's nearly 350 million, but the two countries are similar in size. So the comparison is worth considering.

In a recent development, brazil moves fast. The PAHO asks countries to respond within 72 hours of a suspected measles case. Here's Brazil's own rule:.

According to recent reports, it has also made hunting for cases a national habit. In a program called "Dia S," health workers knock on doors and visit schools, daycare centers and churches to find people who may be sick but have not seen a doctor.

Brazil also holds mass vaccination days called "Dia D." There was one in November, in the area where Brazil borders Colombia and Peru.

If someone is diagnosed with measles, health workers try to track down every person the patient may have met ("contact persons") and vaccinate them and other people living nearby.

The country has so far provided more than 16 million doses of the measles vaccine in 2026 and has donated 500,000 doses to Peru.

Brazil isn't perfect, though. According to official estimates from the World Health Organization, only 76% of children got both required doses of the vaccine in 2025 — well short of the 95% target. Experts warn this leaves the country at risk because measles is so highly contagious. A country needs to be as close to 100% immunized as possible to protect people and stop the disease from spreading.

Industry observers note that "Elimination is not a trophy that we win once and put on a shelf. It must be protected every day," says PAHO Director Jarbas Barbosa.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

It has been revealed that the US lost its measles-free status because the PAHO found that the same strain of the virus had been spreading in the country for 12 months or more. Mexico and Bolivia lost their status on the same day as the US.

The US has had more than 5,400 cases in 2026 (at time of writing), more than twice as many as in all of 2025, and about 19 times as many as in 2024. Nearly everyone who got sick with measles was unvaccinated or had an unknown vaccination status.

US President Donald Trump signed an executive order on latest vaccination recommendations for children in August 2026. It came at a time, when, as we reported, experts mentioned people had stopped getting vaccinated against measles because infection rates were low. But like PAHO's Barbosa said, neglecting vaccination when infection rates are low is a mistake.

To be fair, Trump's executive order listed the measles vaccine in a top category of vaccinations recommended for every child. But the administration's stance on vaccination in general is unclear.

Recent findings suggest that health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has often declared opposition to vaccination, including against measles, advising people to take vitamin A instead. In Texas, this led to children being hospitalized with toxic levels of the supplement, and left them with no protection against measles.

Before the COVID-19 pandemic, 95% of US kindergartners had their measles shots. Now, it's 92%, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Protection (CDC). That leaves about 280,000 kindergartners in the US unprotected.

In the Texas counties where a 2025 measles outbreak began, coverage was as low as 77% at the time.

US children usually need vaccines to start school, but most states let parents opt out for religious or personal reasons, with no doctor involved.

But vaccination rates have fallen elsewhere in the world as well, including in Europe. In Germany, where measles infections have also risen, experts blame anti-vaccination rhetoric that emerged during the COVID-19 pandemic.

A person sick with measles can infect up to18 other, unprotected people. With vaccination, it is possible to increase the number of protected people and lower the number of people the sick person can infect.

To prevent a measles outbreak, a community needs about 95% of people to be vaccinated and/or immune. The vaccination consists of two doses of the MMR (measles, mumps, rubella) vaccine.

But even after the two doses, a person can expect to have only 97% protection against measles — 3% short of full protection — so, nearly everyone in the community has to be vaccinated to keep the average level of protect as close to 100% as possible.

"For some diseases like measles, even a small decrease in vaccination rates can lead to more outbreaks of disease [so] community immunity requires over 95% of susceptible individuals to be immunized," says Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics.

And the 95% has to hold everywhere. A good national average can be affected by, for example, a single school where only 70% of the children are vaccinated. And that is where the outbreak is likely to start.

Around the world, measles deaths have dropped by 88% since 2000, thanks to vaccines.

But progress has stalled. Only about three out of four children worldwide get both doses of the vaccine. The biggest outbreaks right now are in Bangladesh, Indonesia and Guatemala.

Data from Europe indicates that things can get better. In the European Union, cases fell from more than 35,000 in 2024 to about 2,300 the following year, with no measles-related deaths.

Romania went from more than 30,000 cases in 2024 to about 4,200 in 2025.

In Hungary, where 99% of children are vaccinated, there have been no measles cases in the past year.

But in January, six European countries lost their measles-free status, including the UK, Spain and Austria. Across Europe, eight out of ten people who got measles in 2025 were unvaccinated.

Recent findings suggest that the Americas are seeing a major surge in measles infections, with more than 58,000 cases in 2026, over four times as many as by November in 2025. Guatemala has been hit hardest, with almost 35,000 cases.

The deadliest outbreaks are in Africa. African Union countries have so far reported nearly 1,800 measles deaths in 2026, about 1,650 of them in Democratic Republic of Congo. Yet, Sudan, despite the war, raised first-dose measles coverage by 22 percentage points in 2025, which was the world's largest gain.

Industry observers note that measles is extremely contagious. One person can infect up to 18 unprotected people, which makes it about 12 times more contagious than the flu.

According to recent reports, the virus can linger in the air for up to two hours after a sick person has left the room. And people spread it before they know they are sick. Someone with measles is contagious for four days before the rash appears and four days after.

It's not just a rash. About one in five unvaccinated people who get measles in the US ends up in the hospital. Measles can weaken the immune system for years, making it harder to fight off other infections.

But it's preventable. Two doses of the MMR vaccine (which also protects against mumps and rubella) protect 97% of people for life.

This is Nico Paz’s third season in Como. The Azzurri re-signed him from Real Madrid last summer for €60m.

Breaking: Better educated than ever — yet Germany's Gen Z is being shut out of its own future

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1045 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, it is becoming increasingly difficult for young people in Germany to find a job after finishing university or professional training.
  • Furthermore, young people do not feel that politicians are taking action on challenges that matter to them, such as climate protection.
  • What particularly infuriates many young people is being talked about rather than spoken to.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, it is becoming increasingly difficult for young people in Germany to find a job after finishing university or professional training. And finding an affordable place to live in a massive city, and finally starting to live independently is becoming almost impossible.

Furthermore, young people do not feel that politicians are taking action on challenges that matter to them, such as climate protection. The climate conference in Antalya, Turkey, is a case in point. It, therefore, shouldn't be a surprise that young people across Europe once again took to the streets this Friday, which was World Children's Day too, to make their voices heard. In Germany, Gen Z protests took place in 73 towns and cities.

What particularly infuriates many young people is being talked about rather than spoken to. Equally infuriating is seeing their protests branded as criminal before they have even begun, all because of the actions of a small minority.

One example of such rhetoric was when the youth wing of the conservative Christian Democratic Union/Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) party in Berlin-Mitte suggested deploying the German army against demonstrations.

It can also be seen in the media, such as when Bild, Germany's highest-circulation tabloid, ran a headline that translated as: "Young, male, known to the police — who rioted after the demonstrations and where chaos threatens today.".

"Young people are taking to the streets because they feel they are not being heard. And, of course, that feeling is strongly reinforced when the press devotes no more than a brief paragraph to their demands while focusing the rest of its coverage on how these protests could become problematic," states Erik Sczygiol, who until recently was deputy secretary-general of the Federal Conference of Student Representatives. "Of course, any potential security concerns need to be addressed, but they should not overshadow media coverage of the protests.".

The 18-year-old Sczygiol is almost an exception. He was invited to participate in the launch of the World Population Report in Bonn alongside representatives of the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) and the German Foundation for World Population (DSW). This year's report, entitled "Succeeding Generations: Empowering young people to chart the future," is particularly noteworthy because it focuses on Gen Z.

Sources indicate that UN researchers surveyed 109,000 people across 73 countries for the report, some of whose findings are encouraging. Young people worldwide are better educated than any generation before them, with 78% of adolescents across the globe completing at least lower secondary education. But finding a job is becoming increasingly difficult, while informal employment is on the rise.

Recent findings suggest that this economic uncertainty has far-reaching consequences for young people. According to the report, people often do not achieve financial independence until they are in their mid-to-late 20s, and a stable partnership and parenthood are often not realities before their early-to-mid 30s.

Nor do young people have a seat at the political decision-making table when it comes to shaping future reforms in the labor market, housing or climate protection. Florian Brod, 25, points out: "Almost half of the world's population is under 30, yet only 2.6% of parliamentarians worldwide are under 30.".

In a recent development, young people need and want change to protect their livelihoods and those of future generations. "Yet those who will have to live longest with the consequences of today's decisions are precisely the ones who have hardly any representation in the political decision-making process," notes Brod.

He is somewhat close to the political decision-making process as he has served as a Youth Delegate for Sustainable Development for almost two years. In this role, he represents the interests of young people in Germany at United Nations conferences. This is certainly an important step towards giving his generation a greater say in political processes.

Recent findings suggest that nevertheless, both Brod and Sczygiol have had similar experiences. They often participate in conferences and panel discussions and are invited to submit their opinions, but these invitations often amount to little more than symbolic gestures.

"Having access to an international conference is a first step. But without substantive briefings ahead of the conference, without involvement in preliminary negotiations and, in some cases, without access to negotiation texts, there is little opportunity for us to help shape the outcome. When young people see their demands making little headway politically while they are simultaneously excluded from the search for solutions, frustration inevitably builds," states Brod.

Sczygiol adds: "We often get the feeling at the Federal Youth Conference that we were invited simply to provide a nice photo opportunity. We may be sitting at the table, but often only once a bill has already gone through 17 different drafts and is just days away from its final vote in the Bundestag. By that stage, young people have virtually no say in changing anything, and their voices are barely heard. Their contributions are often simply dismissed with: 'Well, that's just typical youthful nonsense.' And that is something that really frustrates young people.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Medical student Amelie Belosevic knows that feeling all too well. She served as Germany's Youth Delegate at the World Health Assembly in Geneva in May. Twenty-five countries sent youth representatives, which Belosevic sees as a clear step forward. However, she has one criticism. According to the United Nations Population Fund, 90% of the world's 1.8 billion young people live in the Global South. Yet, the region was represented by only eight delegates. As a result, Africa, Latin America and large parts of Asia were left virtually voiceless.

According to recent reports, her demands for Germany include better job prospects for young people entering the workforce and sustainable pension systems 40 years from now. "For a very long time, people have mentioned 'I believe my children will have a better life than I do.' But that is no longer necessarily true. So it makes sense then that those who feel the greatest anxiety about the future are the people who have most of their life ahead of them. Sometimes, people don't understand that. We young people need to be able to believe in our future again!".

  • But so far Garnacho has made just seven appearances for the club, and fresh speculation around his future emerged this week after he was left out of the matchday squad for the Champions League clash with Galatasaray, despite Unai Emery naming two goalkeepers on the bench and filling just 11 of his 12 substitute spots.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Aston Villa are open to cutting short Alejandro Garnacho's loan deal from Chelsea in January after he fell down the pecking order, according to The Athletic.

The Argentina winger made the move to Villa Park in the summer on an initial season-long loan deal, with an obligation to make the move permanent next summer based on a select number of appearances being made.

But so far Garnacho has made just seven appearances for the club, and fresh speculation around his future emerged this week after he was left out of the matchday squad for the Champions League clash with Galatasaray, despite Unai Emery naming two goalkeepers on the bench and filling just 11 of his 12 substitute spots.

Now it has emerged that Villa are exploring the possibility of letting Garnacho leave the club in January, according to Jacob Tanswell.

It has been revealed that the deal with Chelsea includes no January break clause, and the Blues have no intention of taking him back at this stage. However, there is hope from Villa that Garnacho and Chelsea could strike an agreement for him to go elsewhere, and they would then be happy to see him move on as he does not presently feature in their plans.

Any exit would hinge on another side finding a solution for the 22-year-old, who has previously played for Manchester United and Chelsea in the last two seasons.

Speaking after the defeat to Galatasaray in midweek, Emery admitted that Garnacho was not someone he was counting on at this stage of the campaign.

"Today the players who were here are who I think are the best players to be here with us.".

Villa cancelling the loan deal would also end any chances of a permanent deal going through in the summer, which is reportedly expected to cost £42.5m should the obligation be triggered.

In a recent development, the Midlands side had a similar situation with Liverpool and Harvey Elliott last season, which ultimately ended with the England youth international sitting on the sidelines for much of the campaign before returning to Anfield in the summer. It now seems that they are looking to avoid that situation from happening again by finding a way to cut this arrangement short.

When Garnacho arrived during the summer, there was hope that Emery could wave his magic wand and get the winger back to the form which saw him being a regular starter for Man Utd under Erik ten Hag.

But it's clear that there are problems beyond what is happening on the pitch with him, having struggled to assert himself anywhere since falling out of favour at Old Trafford.

According to recent reports, villa are not in the best position financially, so they don't want to waste money on players that won't help the team. With Emery having full control at the club, it's clear that unless there is a major U-turn on Garnacho, he has no future at the club, and therefore signing him permanently would make no sense.

We have seen with the Elliott situation last season that the manager has no concern with leaving him out for the rest of the season and not using him, so it's best for everyone involved that a solution is found in January for him to go elsewhere and play.

Bukayo Saka has once again shown why he is one of English footballâs most admired figures, taking time out to donate over a thousand school uniforms to families struggling with the cost of living crisis.

Hailing from Ealing, Saka gifted the uniforms to four local schools, including Greenford High, where he studied as a youngster.

The Arsenal and England winger visited the school personally to surprise pupils, posing for photos, signing autographs, and helping distribute the uniforms to those in need.

According to recent reports, sharing images of the day on Instagram, Saka wrote: "Special day going back home to launch our school uniform project. Thank you to all the schools, our partners and everybody else who helped us give to the students.".

Meanwhile, Outside Greenford High stands a striking mural of Saka, painted in 2021 at the suggestion of a student, celebrating his rise from local schoolboy to football star.

Breaking: China’s AI-powered smart-city model is going global

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (966 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • To understand the Chinese smart city, it helps to know that twenty-first-century infrastructure, technology and policy increasingly makes the whole of China a single, interconnected economic unit.
  • Sources indicate that so, if the goal of a ‘smart city’ is to use big data and AI to outsource governance functions, keeping everything running smoothly, then maybe we should think of China as a single city, with its different provinces and megalopolises as neighbourhoods with their own special roles.
  • In a recent development, china’s 15th five-year strategy unveiled earlier this year sees the country in this way, too, by entrusting certain functions to different cities and regions, and with rural areas also playing an essential role.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

To understand the Chinese smart city, it helps to know that twenty-first-century infrastructure, technology and policy increasingly makes the whole of China a single, interconnected economic unit. Trains, planes and autonomous vehicles shuttle about, with the centre of megacities such as Shanghai and Shenzhen merely being in the middle of ‘one-hour circles’ for commuters that allow them to reach anywhere in the wider urban area with ease. Previous barriers to the internal movement of workers, such the hukou system, which restricted access to public services based on a person’s birthplace, are being removed, making it easier for people to compete for jobs across the country. And all the while, the Internet supercharges these shifts to a nationwide marketplace, backed by an ever-expanding supply of data centres. Sichuanese farmers of organic lemons now livestream from rural villages on apps such as Xiaohongshu or Douyin as they compete for city restaurateurs to buy their products.

Sources indicate that so, if the goal of a ‘smart city’ is to use big data and AI to outsource governance functions, keeping everything running smoothly, then maybe we should think of China as a single city, with its different provinces and megalopolises as neighbourhoods with their own special roles. For instance, three of China’s megacities each have their own notable function: Beijing regulates and invests in fundamental research; Shanghai is home to multinational corporations, frontier research in AI and biotech, and finance; and the Greater Bay Area, including Shenzhen and Guangzhou, is home to innovative manufacturers, such as electric vehicle producer BYD, tech giant Huawei and consumer electronics firm DJI.

Nature Index 2026 Science cities.

Nature Index 2026 Science cities.

In a recent development, china’s 15th five-year strategy unveiled earlier this year sees the country in this way, too, by entrusting certain functions to different cities and regions, and with rural areas also playing an essential role. In the northeast, farming is increasingly carried out with the use of drones and substantial data by state-owned companies such as Beidahuang. In Inner Mongolia and Xinjiang, data centres are powered by abundant solar and wind energy, where they calculate how the self-driving cars of China’s eastern seaboard should navigate roads or process the AI that helps to keep the country’s state-of-the-art high-speed train network running on time.

In a recent development, this approach on data is embodied by 东数西算 (roughly translated as ‘east data, west compute’), a national-level strategic project to channel data from developed eastern regions to resource-rich western regions for processing and storage using eight data-centre ‘hubs’ located across the country. Eastern megacities generate the vast majority of China’s data and AI requests, but they bring skyrocketing land costs, power shortages and cooling difficulties that make hosting data centres unattractive. Instead, the solar farms of Xinjiang’s deserts and the wind farms of the Mongolian steppe are used to provide renewable, cheap energy to data centres.

One key example is Ulanqab in Inner Mongolia, which has been transformed from a traditional farming region into a prominent data powerhouse, earning the name ‘Grassland Cloud Valley’. The energy costs in Ulanqab are low, because the government has been installing massive renewable capacity, relying on the area’s abundant wind and solar resources. Mongolia is cold for most of the year, so data centres use standard air cooling rather than massive air-conditioning set-ups — effectively, they just cover the servers with plastic and leave the door open for wintry winds to circulate. Major firms such as Huawei, Alibaba, Kuaishou and Apple have constructed large-scale cloud bases in Ulanqab. The region houses China’s largest intelligent computing centre for autonomous driving (Fuyao), built by Xpeng Motors and Alibaba Cloud, which has helped make it 170 times faster to train self-driving models. It means an autonomous taxi driving around Beijing is effectively being controlled by servers in the far-away desert of Inner Mongolia.

Mauricio Pochettino ordered Manchester United’s non-starters to complete an extra pitchside weights session immediately after the full-time whistle following Wednesday night’s dramatic 2–2 UEFA Champions League draw against Sporting CP.

The Argentine manager is renowned for his demanding approach to physical conditioning, and there were already signs of his methods being implemented following the full-time whistle in Lisbon.

Several of United’s non-starters were spotted taking part in an additional weights session on the pitch at the Estádio José Alvalade immediately after the game.

Among those involved were Matthijs de Ligt, Luke Shaw, Mason Mount and Andrey Santos, with the players using dumbbells and other conditioning equipment.

It has been revealed that BBC Sports Live: “Some of Manchester United’s non-starters were out on the pitch doing a weights session after tonight’s game. Mauricio Pochettino must feel that fitness has an key part to play if performances are to improve.”.

Despite suffering a humiliating 4-0 defeat to Liverpool in Pochettino’s first game in charge on Sunday, there were considerably more encouraging signs from United against Sporting.

The Red Devils looked sharper going forward, particularly after the interval, when Pochettino reportedly demanded greater aggression and more forward runs from his players.

Bruno Fernandes responded by scoring twice in the space of three minutes against his former club.

The Portuguese international converted a 48th-minute penalty before producing a delightful lob over Sporting goalkeeper Kaique Pereira in the 50th minute to turn the game on its head.

United’s attacking movement and willingness to commit players forward offered an encouraging glimpse of what Pochettino could bring to the team with more time on the training ground.

Ultimately, United were left wondering how they did not leave Portugal with all three points.

After Senne Lammens spilled a routine 80th-minute cross to gift Luis Suárez a second equaliser, United thought they had snatched an 83rd-minute winner when Kaique Pereira flapped Fernandes’ corner into his own net, only for VAR to controversially rule it out for a soft foul by Patrick Dorgu on the goalkeeper.

Combined with Youri Tielemans’ harsh stoppage-time second yellow card, Pochettino’s side were deeply unfortunate not to celebrate their first victory of the new era.

  • Sources indicate that just ask Matt Le Tissier and he'll insist that there's plenty of time to think about anything and everything in life after football.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that footballers are a strange breed, aren't they? Whether it's screaming Ballon d'Or several times down a microphone as if in some kind of Vinicius Junior trance, slapping yourself live on Sky Sports after another Manchester United defeat, or even talking to water. Yes, talking to water.

Sources indicate that just ask Matt Le Tissier and he'll insist that there's plenty of time to think about anything and everything in life after football. For some, that means starting major businesses and dominating the podcast industry. For others, it means grabbing their closest tin foil hats and beginning life as a conspiracy theorist.

It's fair to say that Rickie Lambert falls into the latter category.

Industry observers note that before life on the conspiracy frontline, Lambert was leading the line for Southampton, Liverpool and England, enjoying time with Steven Gerrard and Wayne Rooney as teammates. The forward rapidly became one of the surprise packages in the Premier League as a late-bloomer who found his feet and earned a dream move to boyhood club Liverpool.

It wasn't an easy rise to the top, however. At 23 years old, Lambert was still in the lower tiers of the EFL, playing for Rochdale and Blackpool in League One and League Two.

Sources indicate that it wasn't until Southampton came calling in 2009 that he made his Championship debut at 29. Even he may have settled for that. No one predicted what would happen next.

After almost a decade, the forward finally made his Premier League debut at 30 years old, playing a crucial role for Southampton.

Industry observers note that from the depths of the EFL, Lambert became Mr Reliable for the Saints, scoring 15 Premier League goals in his debut campaign before 13 in the next. Things then got even better when he made his England debut in 2013 and scored the winning goal against Scotland. Lambert was in dreamland.

It has been revealed that it was enough to earn interest from boyhood club Liverpool, who snapped up Lambert's signature in 2014 for around £4m. While he then went onto underwhelm at Anfield, no one can deny that the striker lived the dream when many thought it was already out of reach.

Lambert enjoyed a heroic career. He could have taken the usual route into punditry or coaching in the aftermath of that career. Instead, when COVID-19 struck, he dived head first into the world of conspiracy theories. He joined the likes of Le Tissier by taking to social media with some interesting takes.

The former Liverpool man later described himself as a "critical thinker" and posted in protest of lockdowns during the pandemic.

In 2024, he then aimed a dig at Gary Neville and the former Manchester United right-back's push for an independent football regulator, replying by saying: “Instead of using the footballing community to come together and stop what is being implemented onto us, you are using your position to try and persuade them to accept the corrupt, cowardly shadow government's plan to destroy our way of life and society.”.

Neville simply brushed off Lambert's response, posting: “You ok Rickie?” alongside two crying laughing emojis.

His most absurd theory came in 2023, however. Lambert claimed that, by talking positively to water and be grateful towards it, you could make it clean. He even claimed that scientists have done tests to prove it.

It has been revealed that "They’ve [scientists] done a test where you spoke positively to one glass of water, froze it, spoke negatively to another glass of water, froze it. Then [they] examined the ice. The negativity water was full of holes and blackness. The glass of water that was spoke to positively was full of crystals.".

Coincidentally, Lambert also scored 31 goals with his head throughout his career.

When he's not baffling fans with his conspiracy theories, Lambert has been working towards becoming a coach. In 2023, he became a part-time youth development coach at Wigan Athletic. As of 2026, there has been no announcement of his departure, but it remains unknown whether he is still in the role.

Recent findings suggest that away from coaching, Lambert is also regularly a podcast guest on platforms such as Saints Social, After The Final Whistle and Le Pod by Le Tissier. He also makes speaking appearances, plays in charity games, and is presently the vice-president at Newport IW on the Isle of Wight.

Fans can also see his conspiracy theories across social media, as they await his next bizarre opinion seemingly backed by science.

Published: 03:16 EST, 26 November 2026 | Updated: 06:39 EST, 26 November 2026.

Joshua Kimmich has hammered his own club Bayern Munich for their 'incomprehensible' and 'unacceptable' undermining of Jamal Musiala's ongoing illness battle.

Musiala, the 23-year-old golden boy of German football, has hardly played this season due to seizures brought on by 'neurological dysfunction' and has an £18m-a-year salary until 2030.

Last week, Bayern board member Karl-Heinz Rummenigge suggested the club could discuss him taking a pay cut, arguing: 'We need to talk to the family, the player, and the agency, because then these sums of money, sorry, with all due respect, are no longer feasible.

‘I cannot imagine that Jamal wants to leave the club or that any other club would buy him under these conditions.'.

There was a huge outcry after Rummenigge's remarks, with the likes of Jude Bellingham, Michael Olise and Rio Ferdinand all backing Musiala.

And when asked about the situation after Bayern's 2-1 defeat by Lille in the Champions League on Wednesday night, Kimmich said: 'What happened now is something that simply must never happen in this way. I find it completely incomprehensible.

Joshua Kimmich hammered Bayern Munich for their handling of Jamal Musiala's situation.

Musiala came off the bench for Bayern in their 2-1 defeat by Lille on Wednesday night.

'I think this is something that should be discussed behind closed doors, something you can address with Jamal's agent or with Jamal himself. And I think the other side is open to that as well.

'I believe I've also read that they've met and are supposed to matter a statement. What I don't understand is the way this is being communicated publicly. It must never happen that a player is made to bear the brunt of it.

'Of course, the club always comes first and is bigger than us as players, but it's not bigger than the person. And that's an absolute no-go. It's also not the Bayern way. Especially at this particular time, when I've often emphasised how special this club is.

It has been revealed that 'Even in my own situation, the club was incredibly special. You could really feel that this sense of togetherness was being lived out.'.

Kimmich pointed out that Musiala's health problems are in no way a result of him being unprofessional.

'We mustn't forget that he underwent another operation in the summer and then suffered another injury afterwards,' he continued.

'But I see him and spend time with him every day. I see how he works and how hard he works. That's another crucial aspect of the situation. It's not as though he's having problems because he's unprofessional. Quite the opposite: he's here every day, naturally wants to get the very best out of himself, works extremely hard every day and, I think, genuinely enjoys being part of our team.

'I hope he knows that all of us are 100% behind him, both the team and the club officials.'.

While Kimmich offered his support to Musiala, he admitted he did understand the difficulty the club faces financially with one of their most expensive players unable to start more than one Bundesliga game this season.

Musiala collapsed on the pitch at two consecutive games in August (pictured being helped by team-mates against RB Leipzig).

Industry observers note that he continued: 'Generally speaking, you have to look at the situation from different perspectives. I have absolute understanding for the fact that this is not an easy situation for a club either.

'Of course, I've witnessed Jamal's journey over the past two years. I mean, he carried us at the Euros and was our standout player afterwards. Then he signed a contract extension, was given the number 10 shirt here and with the German national team. Then came the first muscle injury. I can speak from personal experience: when you extend your contract, especially at that age, it's not about sitting back and enjoying the next five years.

'Rather, it's a source of motivation and a responsibility you want to live up to. Then Jamal had the illness and the serious injury. We mustn't forget that over the past year and a half, I don't think he's managed to play four or five games in a row.

'So it's understandable to some extent that he's not performing at his usual level. And it's also understandable that the club might be concerned because of the illness.'.

The Germany international was diagnosed over the summer with absence seizures, a form of epilepsy which causes 'brief but easily treatable seizures'.

Musiala shocked the sporting world when he collapsed in two matches earlier this season, with Bayern manager Vincent Kompany explaining that the player had suffered from a reaction to a change in his medication.

Honorary president Uli Hoeness was the first to speak out on the potential drop-off in form Musiala might suffer with long-term absences, claiming earlier this month that he 'may never regain the performance level he once had'.

'We are facing a dilemma in this case, as he is suffering from an illness that cannot simply be cured, but it can be controlled to a certain extent with the use of medication,' Hoeness told German outlet BR24.

Both Uli Hoeness and Karl-Heinz Rummenigge have made comments suggesting consequences should Musiala not return to his level.

Chief executive Jan-Christian Dreesen then backed up Hoeness's comments and implied that Musiala's contract may need to be 'assessed'.

'We're monitoring his level of play. He'll certainly need time to improve further – like any injured player,' Dreesen said in discussion with AZ. 'And then we need to calmly assess the situation and, if necessary, sit down with his family and management.

'Either we'll all be happy together and he'll be the same Jamal he always was – or, if he's a different Jamal along the way, we'll have to discuss it.'.

It has been revealed that 'If we're not consistently at a level that also aligns with the economic realities, then we'll have to talk to each other. Nevertheless, we have a valid contract, and that's the end of it.'.

The 23-year-old is one of Bayern's highest-earners, having signed a deal with the club to extend his time in Bavaria in February 2025.

Adding fuel to the fire days later was former CEO Karl-Heinz Rummenigge, who told Sky Sports/RTL that he thought it was almost reasonable to discuss a renegotiation should Musiala not return to the level at which he once played.

But the player union Fifpro were forthright in their disagreement with his statements,  releasing a statement claiming that all parties right now sharing their views on Musiala's contract 'should know better'.

'Bayern's honorary president, chief executive and former chief executive have all publicly questioned Musiala's contract in quick succession,' the statement read.

Sources indicate that 'In Fifpro's view, this is a co-ordinated strategy to put pressure on Musiala and his representatives ahead of any negotiations. A club of Bayern's standing should know better.'.

When this statement was shared to social media via journalist Fabrizio Romano, global talents including Jude Bellingham and Musiala's team-mate Michael Olise were among those to like the post.

Criticisms were even more fiery in Germany, with the vice president of Germany's player union Michael Franz accusing the club of harassment.

'What the Bayern Munich officials are doing, and I don't mean Kompany and (Max) Eberl (director of sport), who have behaved impeccably, seems despicable to me,' Franz shared in an interview with Sport1. 'There is even something about it that resembles harassment.'.

Sources indicate that 'A footballer's level of performance can be discussed publicly, but it is not right to talk about his illness and the salary he receives in such circumstances. We must not forget that Jamal Musiala has done everything in his power to come back.'.

'Money has become more key than the person, and that is unacceptable.'.

Musiala collapsed twice within four days in mid-August, first during Bayern's match against Leipzig – shortly after scoring – and then against Heidenheim.

He then returned to the pitch in September, netting against Bodo/Glimt in Champions League action and Union Berlin shortly before the first international break.

After suffering a hamstring injury, Musiala then spent time away from the side before his return at the end of last week – a match which also saw Harry Kane suffer an ankle injury which will keep him out for over three months.

Musiala came off the bench on Wednesday night against Lille and managed to play the final 15 minutes of the 2-1 defeat.

Tech Report: Has the 'Parthenon puzzle' been solved? The long quest to reassemble lost eastern pediment

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (944 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The 2,500-year-old Parthenon is ancient Greece's most important temple and is regarded as one of the greatest masterpieces of the High Classical period of Greek art.
  • Dedicated to Athena, the city's patron goddess, it towers over Athens from its position on the Acropolis — a powerful symbol of the city's importance.
  • Recent findings suggest that the Parthenon had a lasting influence on Western ideas of humanity and art.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The 2,500-year-old Parthenon is ancient Greece's most important temple and is regarded as one of the greatest masterpieces of the High Classical period of Greek art.

Dedicated to Athena, the city's patron goddess, it towers over Athens from its position on the Acropolis — a powerful symbol of the city's importance.

Recent findings suggest that the Parthenon had a lasting influence on Western ideas of humanity and art. The sculptures adorning its pediments, created under the direction of the legendary sculptor Phidias, are considered unparalleled examples of proportion and grace. They have influenced artists from ancient Rome through Neoclassicism to the modern era.

The east pediment above the temple entrance depicted the birth of the goddess Athena from the head of her father Zeus, surrounded by the Olympian gods. A total of 39 figures adorned the roughly 29-meter-long work of art. At its center stood a colossal Zeus figure, measuring 3.8 meters in height.

For centuries, scholars have puzzled over exactly what the arrangement looked like, as the pediment was destroyed during the Christianization of Greece.

But now there has been a breakthrough.

After decades of painstaking detective work and with the help of modern technology, archaeologist Vinzenz Brinkmann and his team have managed to piece together all the surviving fragments of the Parthenon's east pediment.

Recent findings suggest that brinkmann heads the Antiquities and Asia department at Frankfurt's Liebieghaus sculpture collection. "We're very, very confident that we've solved the mystery," he told DW.

The results are now on display in an exhibition at the Liebieghaus titled "Athena, the Stage is Yours: The Parthenon Puzzle.".

Sources indicate that only around 20% of the original marble sculpture's volume is known to have survived. The fragments are scattered across various European museums, with most located in Athens. The British Museum also holds numerous pieces.

Brinkmann and his wife, Ulrike Koch-Brinkmann, have spent more than 40 years working on this ancient puzzle, with so many of its pieces missing.

And they were far from the first to attempt it: "Already in the 19th century, many scholars studied the subject and developed well-founded theories based on their deep knowledge of ancient sources," Brinkmann explains.

Industry observers note that in 1910, a study documenting the many fragments held by the British Museum was published. The research team was able to build on that earlier work, but progress remained slow for years.

It has been revealed that then, in 2014, a visit to the Hermitage Museum in St. Petersburg provided Brinkmann with a crucial clue. There, he encountered a Roman sarcophagus featuring a relief of Athena's birth. "That's when it suddenly clicked: They're all there!".

Industry observers note that nine such sarcophagi are known to exist, almost all of them in Rome. Each depicts a different section of the Parthenon's east pediment.

Sources indicate that brinkmann emphasizes that other scholars had already noticed this connection in the 19th century. "But we really seized on the idea and never let go.".

Recent findings suggest that the researchers also benefited from 21st-century technology: 3D scanners and printers. Brinkmann and his team visited numerous destinations to examine around 60 original fragments at different locations — traveling light. An iPhone was all they needed to scan the pieces.

In a recent development, digitally fitting the fragments together led to another notable discovery. "We know these figures we're putting together!" Brinkmann recalls thinking at the time.

According to recent reports, the Romans had repeatedly made individual copies of all the sculptures from the pediment. "These copies matched the fragments perfectly. Suddenly, we found ourselves surrounded by old acquaintances we had never suspected had come from the pediment." This finally enabled the researchers to reconstruct all the figures and their original arrangement.

According to recent reports, using a 3D printer, the team created a 4-meter-long model at a scale of 1:7.7. For the exhibition, they also produced life-size 3D prints of the most key fragments and mounted them on panels depicting the complete figures at their original size. An animation brings the reconstructed composition to life, digitally assembling the fragments to reveal how the east pediment once looked.

According to recent reports, alongside works from the Liebieghaus collection, the exhibition features loans from other institutions, including the Vatican Museums and the Louvre. Objects from the Acropolis Museum in Athens had originally been expected as well. But Greece withdrew its participation after learning that the British Museum was also planning to lend fragments to the Frankfurt exhibition. The Liebieghaus ultimately decided to forgo the British-owned fragments, too.

Recent findings suggest that there is a reason for this controversy. Britain holds a substantial portion of the Parthenon frieze as well as fragments from both pediments.

Greek authorities have been campaigning for their return for decades.

In Britain, the 56 sections of the frieze are known as the "Elgin Marbles," named after Lord Elgin, the British ambassador to the Ottoman Empire in Constantinople.

In the early 19th century, Elgin had sculptures removed from the exterior of the Parthenon on the Acropolis in Athens. They were taken to Britain with the consent of the Ottoman Empire, which ruled Greece at the time.

Britain maintains that the sculptures were legally acquired.

Greece, however, considers them stolen.

For years, the dispute remained deadlocked. Since the Labour Party came to power in Britain, there has been some movement toward resolving it. But apparently not enough to persuade Greece to lend artworks to an exhibition in which the British Museum might also participate.

The exhibition "Athena, the Stage is Yours. The Parthenon Puzzle" runs through July 25, 2027, at the Liebieghaus in Frankfurt.

This article was originally written in German.

Today is must-win match: for both sides.

For Sunderland that argument is easy to make – they are bottom of the Premier League, are without a win since August and for morale, if nothing else need at least a point, though three is really what the doctor orders.

For Chelsea – fourth in the table and with three wins in their past four league outings – the argument that this is a must-win game is harder to make, but bear with me here...

Facing a Sunderland team who are suffering from the worst of both worlds – blunt in attack and pitiful in defence (what a difference from last season...) and have proven all too easy to beat (as their 2-0 home defeat Zagreb illustrated on Thursday) – the west Londoners are expected to win. Fail to return to the capital with the three points and there will once again be question marks over Xabi Alonso’s side. They are flaky and flashy in equal measure, able to play and win well in spurts, but once again unable to mount sustained pressure needed for a title challenge and forced to battle it out for the hope of a top-four spot at best. Those will be the arguments raised should they not win this afternoon.

Sources indicate that the hosts doubtless wish that their ‘issues’ were as golden as today’s opposition. For Trai Hume, who scored in this fixture last season, the Sunderland players are at fault for the sorry start to the season and he wants to put right the wrongs so far, starting today.

In a recent development, “I couldn’t tell you what’s changed. We thought we’d addressed it after the Leeds game, where we were aggressive, strong, but we go out there tonight and see the old habits of the start of the season. Everything’s a bit laboured, and it’s something the staff can’t fix, it’s on us as players,” Hume mentioned.

“We’re still together as a club, as a team. I think the run of form we’re on, it would be easy to think we’re not, but we are. We are really upset with how we’ve been playing, and the results don’t lie. We haven’t been good enough and we know that. We have to address that.”.

First released in 1995, Mitreâs Ultimax ball quickly became a defining symbol in English football. A fixture on Premier League pitches throughout the 1990s, it made history as the first football to break the 100mph speed barrier.

Now, 30 years later, Mitre has reimagined the legendary ball, bringing it back with a modern twist.

The upcoming Ultimax Pro 30th Anniversary Ball merges the classic design with cutting-edge technology, celebrating its iconic status while setting a new standard for the next generation.

While the ball retains the familiar 6-panel construction, the classic white, blue, and red colourway, and the unmistakable crown logo, itâs been upgraded with advanced features. Hyperflow grooves reduce drag and a sleek pearl finish offers a nod to traditional 30th-anniversary gifts. The interior also sees improvements, with Hyperfoam cushioning now enhanced for cleaner strikes and even more power.

To mark the milestone, Mitre has launched the "The Next In Line" campaign, spotlighting the latest wave of football talent carrying on their family legacies.

The campaign features rising stars such as Raphaella Wright-Phillips, granddaughter of Arsenal icon Ian Wright, Ruben Butt, son of Manchester United legend Nicky Butt, and Jacob Fowler, whose father is Liverpoolâs own Robbie Fowler.

The trio, each in vintage 95/96 kits, embody the connection between the past and the future â just as the latest Ultimax Pro does itself.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that our guts contain around 40 trillion bacterial cells, a similar quantity to the number of cells in the entire human body1.
  • Access Nature and 54 other Nature Portfolio journals.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that our guts contain around 40 trillion bacterial cells, a similar quantity to the number of cells in the entire human body1. Although the community of bacterial species in the human gut usually stays relatively stable over time2, genetic mutations in such bacteria can be associated with a measure of body size called the body mass index3. Writing in Nature, Wang et al.4 scanned the gut bacteria of some 10,000 people for genetic variation and searched for statistically significant associations with almost 250 characteristics, including age, height and cardiovascular fitness. The authors singled out one adaptation that seems to help one of the most abundant bacterial species in the human gut to resist a form of stress called oxidative stress, which damages cells and increases as people age.
